title: Compartment Syndrome
subject: Medicine
summary: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency where swelling raises pressure, compromising blood flow and nerve function. Early recognition and prompt fasciotomy save limb and life.

sections.p: Compartment syndrome occurs when pressure within a closed muscle compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, leading to ischemia. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by pressure measurement if available.
b: Pain out of proportion to injury

t.b: Measures pressure; >30 mmHg or within 30 mmHg of diastolic pressure indicates need for fasciotomy

sections.p: Staging guides urgency: Stage 1 – pain only; Stage 2 – pain + paresthesia; Stage 3 – motor deficit; Stage 4 – irreversible damage.
In low‑resource settings, the commonest causes are crush injuries, fractures, burns, and tight bandages. Infections such as tetanus or severe cellulitis can also precipitate it.

t.b: Establishes timing and mechanism; early onset suggests acute compartment

sections.p: Patients report severe pain that worsens with passive movement. Sensory loss precedes motor loss. Pulses may remain palpable until late stages.
In many East African hospitals, pressure monitoring may be unavailable. Clinical exam remains king; if a portable manometer exists, use it. Lab tests are supportive.

t.b: If unavailable, rely on clinical signs and consider urgent transfer

sections.p: Delayed treatment leads to permanent muscle necrosis, nerve damage, and systemic complications such as rhabdomyolysis and renal failure.
Immediate surgical decompression is mandatory. Supportive care includes fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolytes, and monitoring for systemic effects.
b: Urgent fasciotomy within 6 hours of diagnosis

sections.p: Post‑fasciotomy care involves wound management, physiotherapy, and monitoring for infection. Prevention focuses on early recognition and avoiding tight dressings.

t.b: Prompt re‑intervention if new deficits appear

sections.p: Differential includes deep vein thrombosis, nerve injury, and simple swelling from trauma.
b: Deep vein thrombosis – pain but no passive stretch pain
Nerve injury – sensory loss without pain

sections.p: Normal pulses can be misleading; compartment pressure may be normal in early stages. Lab values may be normal until significant muscle breakdown.
b: Pulses may remain palpable until late

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain out of proportion to injury

faq.q: Can compartment syndrome occur without a fracture?
faq.a: Yes, severe crush injuries, burns, or tight bandages can raise compartment pressure even without bone fractures.

faq.q: What is the threshold pressure that triggers fasciotomy?
faq.a: An intracompartmental pressure >30 mmHg or within 30 mmHg of diastolic pressure warrants urgent fasciotomy.
Delays beyond 6 hours increase the risk of irreversible muscle and nerve damage, leading to permanent loss of function.

exam: A 25‑year‑old man presents with severe leg pain after a crush injury. On exam, pain worsens with passive stretch. What is the next step? — Immediate fasciotomy; do not wait for imaging.
You suspect compartment syndrome but the patient has a tight bandage. What is the first action? — Remove the bandage and reassess neurovascular status.
A patient has normal pulses but severe pain on passive stretch. What does this indicate? — Compartment syndrome; pulses can remain normal until late stages.
You have a portable pressure monitor. The measured pressure is 28 mmHg and diastolic BP is 80 mmHg. What does this mean? — 28 mmHg is within 30 mmHg of diastolic pressure; fasciotomy is indicated.
A patient develops hyperkalaemia after fasciotomy. Which drug should be avoided? — Nephrotoxic agents like aminoglycosides; use alternatives.
You are in a rural clinic without a pressure monitor. How do you decide on fasciotomy? — Rely on clinical signs: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and sensory changes.
